n: Nephi turns from his father’s dream to a new section of his record. He calls it an account of his own “reign and ministry,” written years later after he had become the Nephites’ leader, but he must first finish telling of Lehi and his brothers.

f.g: The small plates of Nephi, a record set apart for sacred things.

n: After describing the tree of life dream, Lehi urged his family to be diligent and then began to prophesy about the Jews back in Jerusalem.

Lehi foresees Jerusalem’s destruction and the Babylonian captivity, then the Jews’ return to their homeland. This happened: Babylon destroyed Jerusalem in 587/586 BC, and Persia’s King Cyrus let the exiles go home about fifty years later.

Lehi gives a precise timeline: the Messiah would come six hundred years after he left Jerusalem. The title “Messiah” means “anointed one,” and Lehi immediately explains it in plain terms — the Savior of the whole world.

f.g: Hebrew mashiaḥ, “anointed one”; in Greek, Christos.

n: Lehi points out that he was not alone: many prophets before him had testified of this coming Redeemer. Testimony of Christ runs through all of scripture.

f.w: how great a number had testified

n: This is why a Redeemer is needed: since the Fall, all people are lost and fallen, and they would stay that way forever unless they rely on Him. It is a short, clear statement of the core of the plan of salvation.

f.w: lost and in a fallen state

n: Lehi also prophesies of a forerunner who would prepare people for the Messiah — the one we know as John the Baptist.

f.w: prepare the way of the Lord

n: Lehi’s words closely match what John the Baptist would actually say six centuries later. A shoe’s “latchet” is its strap; untying a master’s sandals was a servant’s lowliest job, so John is saying he isn’t worthy even to be Christ’s humblest servant.

f.g: The leather strap or thong of a sandal.

n: Lehi even names the place: Bethabara, east of the Jordan River, which is where the Gospel of John says John was baptizing. The prophecy also foresees John baptizing Jesus Himself.

f.g: A crossing place on the Jordan; some manuscripts of John 1:28 read “Bethany beyond Jordan.”

n: After baptizing Jesus, John would testify that He is the “Lamb of God” — a title that recalls the lambs offered in sacrifice and points to Christ’s atoning death for the sins of the world.
Lehi foresees the gospel being preached to the Jews, their rejection of Jesus, His death and resurrection, and then the message going to the Gentiles (non-Israelites) through the Holy Ghost.

f.w: dwindling of the Jews in unbelief
manifest, by the Holy Ghost, unto the Gentiles

n: Lehi uses an olive tree to picture Israel. Its branches broken off and scattered represent Israelite groups — including Lehi’s own family — being separated from the main body of the covenant people.
Lehi sees his family’s journey to a new land as part of this scattering. Their departure is not random; it fulfills God’s plan for scattering Israel throughout the world.

The scattering is not the end of the story. After the Gentiles receive the full gospel, the “natural branches” — remnants of Israel — will be grafted back in by coming to know Jesus as their true Messiah. This is the gathering of Israel.
Nephi notes that Lehi said much more than he records here. Nephi had written more of it in his “other book,” the large plates, which focused on history.

f.g: The large plates of Nephi, the more historical record.

n: All of this teaching took place in the family’s tent camp in the valley of Lemuel, near the Red Sea, early in their journey.

Nephi longs to see and know for himself what his father saw. He explains that Lehi received revelation by the Holy Ghost through faith in Christ, and that this same gift is open to everyone who diligently seeks God.

f.w: desirous also that I might see

n: God does not change. Because He is the same in every age, the path back to Him has been prepared for all people from the beginning, on the same condition: repent and come to Him.

f.w: the same yesterday, today, and forever
from the foundation of the world

n: Whoever seeks diligently will find. God’s “mysteries” — truths known only by revelation — are opened by the Holy Ghost in every era. The phrase “one eternal round” means God’s ways are consistent; He doesn’t play favorites across time.

f.w: he that diligently seeketh shall find

n: Nephi turns to address his reader directly: everything we do will one day be judged.
Mortal life is a “probation,” a testing period. Those who choose wickedness and do not repent will be unclean at the judgment, and nothing unclean can live in God’s presence.

f.g: The time of testing in mortality.

f.w: no unclean thing can dwell with God

n: Nephi closes by explaining why he speaks so boldly: the Holy Ghost has given him authority to say these things, and he will not deny them.
